claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch among constituent elements increases lattice distortion in equiatomic high-entropy alloys.
Greater lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion increases alloy hardness.
Impeded dislocation motion increases alloy strength.
The baseline is an equiatomic, single-phase HEA with moderate atomic size mismatch and a solution-annealed microstructure.
Replacing a constituent element with one having a substantially different atomic radius will increase the alloy's overall atomic size mismatch.
The replacement can be performed while retaining an equiatomic composition.
Enhanced atomic size mismatch induces greater lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion creates additional obstacles to dislocation motion.
Greater lattice distortion increases dislocation pinning.
The modified HEA will have higher nanoindentation hardness than the baseline alloy.
The modified HEA will have higher tensile yield strength than the baseline alloy.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold for single-phase, solution-annealed HEAs tested at room temperature when segregation and secondary-phase formation are negligible.
Elemental segregation or unintended phase formation may alter mechanical properties independently of lattice distortion.
X-ray diffraction measurements of lattice-parameter distribution can be used to evaluate the proposed increase in lattice distortion.
Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in both hardness and yield strength, or failure to observe increased lattice distortion, is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.
